nodes.label: Funder acknowledgments
nodes.one_line: Credit your funders in the places their grant agreements require — websites, materials, events — visibly and promptly.
know_what: the acknowledgment clause in the grant agreement — the exact sentence some funders require on materials, often verbatim with a set placement
funder logo requirements — file formats, color vs mono versions, clear-space minimums, and the prohibition on re-coloring or altering the lockup
the named-credit convention — "generously supported by [Funder]" taglines and how to order multiple funders on a page
digital acknowledgment places: website footer and donor page, email signatures, social posts, and annual report masthead
federal public-acknowledgment language — awards made under federal dollars require specific statements (e.g., "This project was supported by...") and disclaimers of endorsement
the distinction between required acknowledgment (agreement clause) and optional thank-you (which never substitutes for the clause)
know_how: read the grant agreement's acknowledgment clause before celebrating the award, and list every place it names
pull the funder's current logo pack from their brand or grantee portal instead of reusing an old file
place the acknowledgment within the window the agreement sets (often 30-60 days of award) and log the placement
match the funder's stated tagline and language verbatim — do not paraphrase a required credit
when multiple funders support one program, order credits by size or agreement requirement, never by recency
notify the funder before a major announcement or event where they are credited, so they can coordinate
habits: checking every new grant agreement for an acknowledgment clause before doing anything else with the award
keeping a running acknowledgment log: funder, required language, places, date placed, proof screenshot
reviewing the website footer and annual report masthead quarterly for stale or missing credits
flagging new public materials (brochures, reports, event signage) to funders who require advance notice
re-verifying logo files against the funder's brand guide every time a new material is produced
nodes.checkpoint: Place each funder's required acknowledgment (logo and tagline exactly per the agreement) in every named location — website footer, annual report, event signage — within the agreement's stated window, with the placement logged.
nodes.common_failure: Treating acknowledgment as optional cosmetics — funders audit their grantees' visibility and some make a silent credit the first sign of a weak relationship; using an outdated or re-colored logo; paraphrasing required language; crediting on the website but missing the annual report the agreement also names.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Candid — grantee acknowledgment guidance (Candid.org)
Foundation grant agreement templates (e.g., Ford Foundation, Robert Wood Johnson Foundation award letters)

nodes.label: Reporting calendar
nodes.one_line: Track every interim and final report deadline across active grants so no reporting window is ever missed.
know_what: interim vs final reports — many agreements require a mid-grant narrative or financial report, not just a closing one
the two report windows — due-on-period-end vs due-30-60-days-after-period-end — and which each funder uses
report components per funder: narrative, financial statement, SF-425 (Federal Financial Report) for federal awards, and supporting data
the reporting section of the award letter — the authoritative deadline source, not the funder's marketing page
federal monitoring duties under 2 CFR 200.328-200.329, including subrecipient monitoring and the annual closeout timeline
no-cost extension and carryover mechanics, whose approval windows often bind to reporting deadlines
know_how: build the calendar the day each award lands: due date, portal or email, components, and the person who drafts and the person who approves
work backward two weeks from every deadline for the drafting window, and flag conflicts between reports due the same week
distinguish narrative from financial deadlines — they sometimes land on different dates in the same agreement
record the submission portal and login for each funder (Grants.gov, foundation portals, email) so submission is not a scavenger hunt
set reminders at 60, 30, and 7 days out, and treat the 7-day mark as the freeze for drafting
reconcile the calendar monthly with finance so drawdowns and cash requests are not blocked by a missing report
habits: entering reporting obligations into the tracker on award day, never 'later'
trusting the award letter over any third-party listing of deadlines
reviewing the full calendar monthly with the person who signs reports
treating a funder's silence as no signal at all — absence of a reminder is not an extension
logging the submission confirmation so there is proof on file for every report
nodes.checkpoint: Produce a reporting calendar covering every active grant — each report's due date, portal, components (narrative/financial), and owner — with a two-week drafting buffer before every deadline, and update it within a week of any new award.
nodes.common_failure: Relying on funder reminders — many are never sent and some funders penalize lateness or freeze further draws; treating the calendar as a one-time list instead of a living tracker; missing that interim and final reports have different dates; losing portal credentials at deadline time.
sources: 2 CFR 200.328-200.329 (monitoring and reporting)
SF-425 Federal Financial Report instructions (grants.gov)
Candid — grant reporting best practices

nodes.label: Narrative & financial reporting
nodes.one_line: Write progress reports that document outcomes against the proposal's promises and flag problems before funders find them.
know_what: the no-surprise rule — a funder should learn bad news from you, in writing, before they learn it any other way
promised objectives as the report's skeleton — the proposal's SMART objectives are the checklist the report must answer
activity vs outcome reporting — what you did (activities) vs what changed (outcomes), and why funders pay for the second
financial report formats — actuals vs budget, the SF-425 for federal awards, and the variance line a reviewer reads first
the variance explanation convention — every material over- or under-spend line gets a one-line reason, not just a number
evidence attachments — data tables, participant counts, photos with consent, and third-party evaluations that back the narrative claims
know_how: pull the proposal's objectives and outcome measures before drafting, and structure the report objective by objective
quantify every claim with the measure from the evaluation plan — named count, percentage, or instrument score, not 'many'
flag any shortfall or delay on the first page, with the cause and a corrective plan, before the praise
keep narrative and financial figures consistent — the people count in the story must match the headcount in the budget line
write the final report so it doubles as renewal evidence: results, lessons learned, and what the next phase would buy
submit through the agreed channel with confirmation saved, well before the deadline so funder questions have time to breathe
habits: keeping a running evidence file through the grant year, so the report is assembled, not recreated, at deadline
writing the report against the proposal document, never from memory
reporting a problem the week it is known, not the week the report is due
re-reading the previous report before writing the next, so the story is continuous
reusing reported data in the next proposal — what the funder already approved is the strongest evidence you have
nodes.checkpoint: Write a progress report that maps every promised objective to a reported actual with a number, flags any shortfall on the first page with a corrective plan, and matches its financial figures to the budget — submitted before the deadline with confirmation saved.
nodes.common_failure: Writing reports as marketing, so a funder cannot tell what actually changed; hiding problems until the final report, which converts a fixable setback into a trust break; reporting activities instead of outcomes; letting narrative and financial numbers contradict each other; drafting at the deadline so there is no time for the funder's follow-up questions.
sources: 2 CFR 200.328-200.329 (monitoring and reporting)
SF-425 Federal Financial Report instructions (grants.gov)
The Grantsmanship Center — grant reporting articles

nodes.label: Funder relationship
nodes.one_line: Run a funder relationship deliberately — updates, transparency, responsiveness — so the funder knows you between applications, not just at ask time.
know_what: the program officer role — the funder staffer who champions your grant internally; the grants manager who administers it, and why they are different audiences
the check-in cadence convention — a quarterly touchpoint between reports is standard for active grants; silence is not a relationship
responsiveness norms — returning funder email within one business day, and flagging when an answer will take longer
what a program officer can use from you: early results, participant stories with consent, photos, and data they can quote in their own reporting
the transparency norm — sharing a problem early is read as competence; hiding it is read as risk
the single-voice rule — the funder should hear one consistent story from your organization, not conflicting updates from different staff
know_how: schedule a standing check-in with each active program officer (quarterly call or short email) and log what was discussed
respond to funder inquiries within one business day, even if the full answer takes longer
send early wins and early warnings before the report deadline, so the report confirms what the funder already knows
give the program officer quotable material — a stat, a story, a photo — they can reuse in their internal reporting
invite the program officer to relevant events and offer a tailored tour when they visit
keep a relationship log: contacts, preferences (email vs call), staff changes, and what was promised, so the relationship survives turnover
habits: updating the program officer before the report, never using the report as the first contact since the award
tracking each PO's stated preferences and reviewing them before every touchpoint
noting program-officer changes immediately and re-onboarding the new person with a written context memo
never surprising the funder with bad news in a report they could have heard months earlier
reviewing the relationship log before every renewal cycle so the ask lands on a documented history

know_why.claim: Cultivate the funder between grants — regular touchpoints that are not asks — so the renewal is decided on a known, trusted relationship rather than a cold application.
know_why.because: foundation boards fund organizations their program officers can defend, and a PO who has heard your results and your problems firsthand can carry that defense; a documented relationship also survives PO turnover, which otherwise resets you to stranger status.
know_why.disputed_by: the leave-them-alone camp holds that unsolicited contact between grants reads as needy, consumes a PO's limited hours, and that renewal decisions are actually made on the reported results — so cultivation effort is noise at best and a nuisance at worst.
know_why.source: practitioner debate in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine and program-officer commentary at grantee conferences

nodes.checkpoint: Run one mid-grant check-in: send a program officer a short update covering results and one early problem before the scheduled report, respond to their reply within one business day, and log the exchange with their stated preferences.
nodes.common_failure: Treating the funder as a check-writer until the next ask — no contact for a year, then a renewal request that lands cold; or the opposite failure of contacting only to ask, so every touchpoint is a transaction; one staff member hoarding the relationship so it dies with their departure.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
The Grantsmanship Center — grantee-funder relationship guidance
Foundation program-officer panels at GrantSpace webinars (Candid)

nodes.label: Site visits & check-ins
nodes.one_line: Prepare for a funder site visit or check-in so it confirms the story your proposal told instead of undercutting it.
know_what: the site visit as verification, not PR — funders attend to confirm the program exists, operates as proposed, and has the capacity to spend the money well
what funders watch for: fidelity to the proposal, real implementation capacity, staff who can answer specifics, and red flags (empty facilities, staged props, evasive answers)
who to bring — the people who run the work (program staff, frontline workers, finance if asked), not a lineup of executives
the virtual visit norm — since 2020 many check-ins are video calls; the same preparation applies plus tested technology
the unannounced-visit reality — anything you stage must survive a visit you did not schedule, so the staged and the real must match
the 48-hour follow-up convention — thank-you plus every promised document within two business days
know_how: ask the funder what they want to see before building the agenda, and build it to mirror the proposal's claims
prepare evidence for each agenda item: outcome data, participant stories with consent, and the program space itself
brief every staffer who will speak on the proposal's promises and the two or three numbers they must know cold
walk the actual program space before the visit and fix what a visitor would see, without staging anything new
rehearse the Q&A, including the questions you dread, and agree on what not to say (internal politics, unapproved plans)
for virtual visits, test the link, camera, and screen-share a day ahead, and have a phone fallback
send the thank-you and promised materials within 48 hours, and log what was discussed
habits: asking what the funder wants to see before writing a single agenda line
walking the program space as a visitor would before they arrive
briefing every speaker, including the person who only shows one data slide
never staging anything that could not survive an unannounced visit
sending follow-up materials while the visit is still fresh in the funder's memory
nodes.checkpoint: Run a site visit or check-in end to end: an agenda mirroring the proposal's claims, staff who can answer implementation questions in the room, rehearsed evidence for each agenda item, and a follow-up with promised materials sent within 48 hours.
nodes.common_failure: Over-staging — funders see rehearsed performances and can visit unannounced, so the staged version and the real version must match; putting only the executive director in the room, so implementation questions go unanswered; treating the visit as a PR opportunity when the funder is there to verify; leaving a funder question unanswered until it dies.
sources: Candid — preparing for a site visit (GrantSpace)
Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
The Grantsmanship Center — site visit checklists

nodes.label: Renewal & follow-on asks
nodes.one_line: Convert a completed grant into a renewal or expansion ask using reported results as the evidence.
know_what: renewal vs expansion ask — same scope again vs more money or broader scope, and how the evidence burden differs
the reported-results-as-evidence convention — the final report's documented outcomes are the opening argument of the renewal ask
funder renewal mechanics — some foundations renew automatically after a clean final report; others require a fresh competitive application; know which you face
the board-cycle timing constraint — foundation budgets are set in cycles, so a renewal asked after the cycle closes waits a year
the multi-year commitment option — proposing 2-3 years of support at a stepped amount is a legitimate ask, not a given
bridge-funding fallbacks — a reduced-scope or short-bridge request keeps the door open when full renewal is not available
know_how: draft the renewal ask from the final report, quoting its documented outcomes as the evidence base
quantify the delta the grant produced — the before/after the money bought — rather than re-describing the program
propose the next phase with fresh SMART objectives and a specific multi-year structure and amount
time the ask to the funder's board cycle, working back from their decision meetings, typically 3-6 months before the grant ends
run the draft past the program officer before the formal submission, so the first official ask is not a surprise
prepare the fallback in advance: if full renewal is refused, ask what evidence or timing would change the answer
habits: starting the renewal conversation 3-6 months before the grant ends, never after it closes
building the ask from reported data, not from a blank page
tracking which funders renew automatically vs re-compete, and noting it in the pipeline tracker
treating a 'no' as information — ask what would change it and record the answer
never assuming renewal, even after three clean reports

know_why.claim: Ask for renewal only after the final results are reported, so the ask is anchored in documented outcomes rather than promises.
know_why.because: a renewal decision rests on what the money bought, and a program officer cannot defend a renewal to their board without results in hand; asking before results exist forces the funder to decide on faith, which is a weaker ask for everyone.
know_why.disputed_by: the momentum camp argues the opposite: ask early, while the grant is visibly working and the relationship is warm, because foundation boards budget cycles ahead — a late ask can arrive after renewal money was already allocated to someone else, making results moot.
know_why.source: practitioner debate in The Grantsmanship Center Magazine and program-officer commentary at grantee conferences

nodes.checkpoint: Send a renewal request built on the final report's documented outcomes, with a specific multi-year amount and structure, timed to the funder's board cycle and previewed with the program officer before submission.
nodes.common_failure: Assuming renewal and asking for more money with no new evidence; asking after the grant has closed so the funder's budget cycle has passed and the money is already allocated; sending a renewal ask that reads like a first-time proposal, ignoring the documented history; taking a 'no' as final instead of learning what would change the answer.
sources: Karsh & Fox, The Only Grant-Writing Book You'll Ever Need
Candid — renewing foundation grants (GrantSpace)
The Grantsmanship Center — follow-on funding guidance

nodes.label: Impact storytelling
nodes.one_line: Turn reported outcomes into a specific story with a named beneficiary that humanizes the grant for funders and boards.
know_what: the one-named-beneficiary convention — a single specific person's arc humanizes data that a thousand names would blur
informed consent for stories — written permission covering name, photo, and quotes, and the exact materials and audiences each consent covers
photo and video release forms — the model-release standard, including minors' forms requiring a guardian's signature
the story-data pairing — every story is anchored to the reported outcome it illustrates, so the anecdote cannot float free of the evidence
sensitivity situations — survivors of violence, undocumented people, children, and health-service users, where even a consented story can expose someone; anonymity and composite options exist
the consent-lifecycle rule — a consent given for one funder's report does not cover a new funder, a public website, or a national conference
know_how: identify a story that illustrates a reported outcome — a named beneficiary whose arc maps to a data point in the report
obtain written consent before collecting photos or quotes, covering name, likeness, and exact uses, with the beneficiary allowed to read the final text first
store signed consent forms with the story file so every future use can be checked against the permission given
pair the story with its data point in reports and proposals — one paragraph of person, one line of number
re-confirm consent when a use changes: a new funder, a public report, or a press mention each need fresh permission
let the beneficiary approve the final wording, including the photo crop and the quote in context
habits: collecting consent at intake, not after the fact, so the story is ready when a funder asks
checking the consent log before every major use of a story or photo
never embellishing or merging two people's stories into one composite without saying so
keeping stories current — refreshing the archive so a three-year-old story is not doing duty for new funding
checking with the beneficiary before each new high-visibility use, even when consent is on file
nodes.checkpoint: Publish one impact story with a named beneficiary: written consent on file covering name, photo, and quotes for the specific funder use, beneficiary-approved final text, and the story linked to its reported outcome data point.
nodes.common_failure: Using a photo or quote without consent and getting burned — one harm story (an exposed survivor, a misquoted beneficiary) ends the trust that took years to build; embellishing or merging stories until the anecdote no longer matches the data; reusing one story forever until it goes stale; treating the beneficiary as raw material instead of a person with rights over their own story.
sources: Candid — ethical storytelling guidance (GrantSpace)
Andy Goodman, Storytelling As Best Practice
Foundation Center — consent and photo release templates
